summary: Defines the User-based Security Model for SNMPv3, which provides message-level security. It specifies the procedures for authenticating and protecting SNMP messages on a per-user basis, and includes a MIB for remotely managing the model's configuration. It replaces RFC 2574.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a network gadget obeys a command, it should know who sent it and that nobody changed it on the way. This note gives each user a way to prove who they are and keep messages private.

questions: what is the snmpv3 user based security model
how does snmpv3 prevent replay attacks
what is the snmpv3 time window
how does snmpv3 key localization work
subtitle: How SNMPv3 proves who sent a management message, spots tampering and replays, and can hide the contents.

tldr.problem: Network devices accept management commands over SNMP, so an attacker who can alter, forge or replay those messages could change a device's configuration or falsify what it reports.
tldr.mechanism: The User-based Security Model ties secret keys to named users. Each message carries a keyed digest for integrity and authentication, a time indicator from the authoritative engine to reject stale messages, and optionally encrypted contents.
tldr.outcome: SNMPv3 messages can be authenticated, checked for freshness and encrypted per user. The RFC is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2574 and has since been updated by RFC 5590.

today: RFC 3414 is an Internet Standard (STD 62). It obsoletes RFC 2574 and has been updated by RFC 5590; it has not itself been obsoleted.

sections.title: Threats and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 3414 defines the User-based Security Model (USM), the security model used by SNMP version 3. It works at the level of a single message. The main idea is to use the traditional concept of a user, identified by a userName, and to attach security information to that user.

The principal threats are modification of information (altering a message in transit to cause an unauthorized operation) and masquerade (pretending to be a user with the right authorizations). Two secondary threats get limited protection: disclosure (eavesdropping) and message stream modification (malicious reordering, delay or replay). Denial of service and traffic analysis are explicitly out of scope.

The goals follow from this: verify that a message was not modified, verify the identity of the user it claims to come from, detect messages that are not recent, and, when needed, keep the contents from being disclosed. One design constraint is that when effective management in times of network stress conflicts with security, USM prefers the former.
sections.plainLanguage: The note-passing system has to stop three tricks: someone changing a note, someone pretending to be you, and someone showing an old note again. Hiding what the note says is a bonus.

sections.title: Modules and Users
sections.content:
USM is split into three modules. The authentication module provides data integrity and data origin authentication. The timeliness module protects against delay or replay beyond what normal operation causes, and it is fixed for USM. The privacy module protects the message payload from disclosure. Several authentication and privacy protocols can exist side by side, which is why the HMAC-MD5-96, HMAC-SHA-96 and CBC-DES descriptions sit in their own sections and can be replaced or supplemented later.

Each user has a userName, a securityName, an authProtocol and authKey, and a privProtocol and privKey. Keys are not accessible via SNMP. The only way to change them remotely is through the key change objects, which do so securely without needing privacy protection.

The RFC states a hard dependency: there is no confidentiality without both integrity and origin authentication, and neither integrity nor origin authentication is possible without the other. Authentication also identifies the user on whose behalf a message was sent, not the specific originating device.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three helpers: one checks the stamp, one checks the note is fresh, and one puts the note in a locked box. Each person has their own secret stamp and key.

sections.title: Security Parameters in a Message
sections.content:
An SNMPv3 message carries a msgSecurityParameters field, which for USM is an OCTET STRING holding the BER encoding of a sequence of six fields: msgAuthoritativeEngineID, msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots, msgAuthoritativeEngineTime, msgUserName, msgAuthenticationParameters and msgPrivacyParameters.

The boots and time values are integers from 0 to 2147483647. The user name is 0 to 32 octets. A zero-length user name matches no user but can be used for engine ID discovery. The last two fields are defined by whichever authentication and privacy protocols the user has configured.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note gets a little label on the outside: whose engine is in charge, what time it says, who wrote the note, and the proof-of-stamp.

sections.title: Timeliness and Replay Protection
sections.content:
In every exchange one SNMP engine is the authoritative engine. If the message carries a payload that expects a response, the receiver is authoritative. If it does not (a notification, for example), the sender is. The authoritative engine's identity and clock are put in the message, so a message meant for one authoritative engine cannot be replayed to another and a stale message can be spotted.

Each engine keeps snmpEngineID, snmpEngineBoots (reboots since the ID was configured) and snmpEngineTime (seconds since boots was last incremented). Boots is held in non-volatile storage, so no clock needs to tick while the device is off. The same Time Window of 150 seconds applies to all users.

A non-authoritative engine keeps its own copy of the authoritative engine's boots and time, plus latestReceivedEngineTime, and updates them from authentic messages. If an authoritative engine cannot determine its boots value it sets it to 2147483647, where it latches and every authenticated message fails with notInTimeWindow; resetting it needs a physical visit.

The timeliness check is only done when the message is authenticated, so the time values in it can be trusted. Message reordering inside the window is not detected by USM; the RFC points to snmpSetSerialNo for ordering Set operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note says what time the boss's clock showed. If the time on a note is too far off, the robot ignores it as an old note. Everyone gets the same 150 seconds of wiggle room.

sections.title: Passwords and Key Localization
sections.content:
A person has one password but should not share the same secret with every device. USM handles this with key localization. The password is first turned into a key Ku by the algorithm in the appendix. To get the localized key for one authoritative engine, the engine's snmpEngineID is placed between two copies of Ku, and the result is run through the hash function of the user's authentication protocol (MD5 or SHA).

The effect, in the RFC's words, is that it is practically impossible to work out the user's password, or the key for another engine, from any combination of keys held on engines. Disclosure of the password itself still defeats this, so the password or non-localized key MUST NOT be stored on a managed device; only the localized key SHALL be stored, if at all.

If the appendix algorithm is used, passwords must be at least 8 characters. Using the same password, and therefore the same key, for both authentication and privacy is called very poor security practice.
sections.plainLanguage: You remember one password, but each robot gets its own special version made by mixing your password with the robot's name. If one robot is broken into, your other robots are still safe.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Discovery
sections.content:
To send, the engine looks up the user, fails with unknownSecurityName or unsupportedSecurityLevel if the user cannot support what was asked, then optionally encrypts the scoped PDU, fills in the engine ID, boots, time and user name, and finally computes the authentication parameters over the whole message. Authentication is done last because it covers the whole message.

To receive, the engine parses the security parameters, finds the user, checks that the requested security level is supported, verifies the authentication, checks timeliness, and decrypts if needed. Each failure increments a specific counter and returns an error: for example usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs, usmStatsUnknownUserNames, usmStatsUnsupportedSecLevels, usmStatsWrongDigests, usmStatsNotInTimeWindows and usmStatsDecryptionErrors.

A manager does not know a device's engine ID in advance, so discovery comes first. It sends an unauthenticated request with a zero-length user name and engine ID and an empty variable list. The authoritative engine answers with a Report containing its engine ID and the usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs counter. For authenticated communication, a second authenticated request with boots and time set to zero draws a Report with the real boots and time and the usmStatsNotInTimeWindows counter, and time synchronization happens as a side effect of normal receive processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Before talking, the manager knocks and asks "who is in charge here?" The robot answers with its name and what time it is. After that, the manager can send properly stamped notes.

sections.title: The HMAC and DES Protocols
sections.content:
Two authentication protocols are defined. HMAC-MD5-96 computes a 128-bit MD5 digest in HMAC mode over the whole message and carries the first 96 bits (12 octets) of it; the key is 16 octets. HMAC-SHA-96 does the same with a 160-bit SHA digest, again carrying 12 octets, with a 20-octet key. HMAC-MD5-96 is the one that MUST be supported; HMAC-SHA-96 SHOULD be.

The privacy protocol is CBC-DES. The first 8 octets of the 16-octet privacy key are the DES key (the least significant bit of each octet is ignored) and the last 8 octets are a pre-IV. A per-packet 8-octet salt is built from the engine's 32-bit boots value and a local 32-bit counter, XOR-ed with the pre-IV to get the initialization vector, and sent in the privacy parameters so the receiver can decrypt. Data is padded to a multiple of 8 octets and encrypted in Cipher Block Chaining mode.

Privacy is optional to implement; at least one authentication protocol is required for a Secure SNMP implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp is made by mixing the note with your secret and keeping a short fingerprint of the result. The locked box scrambles the note block by block, and each block's scrambling depends on the one before it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends several practices. Responses with no matching outstanding request must be discarded, and an engine using a msgID to match them MUST use different values in all requests sent during a Time Window (150 seconds). Time synchronization should use authenticated messages. A command generator sending state-altering messages should wait for an acknowledgement or for the previous message to expire, because an authenticated message stays valid, and replayable, for roughly 150 seconds.

Secrets should be changed more often the more they are used, and with more caution on public data networks. To be called a Secure SNMP implementation, an implementation MUST implement an authentication protocol, restrict access to user secrets, implement key localization, and implement the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB.

Sending Report PDUs unsecured (noAuthNoPriv) can expose a non-authoritative engine to some attacks. The usmUserTable in the MIB is sensitive, so access to it should be controlled, for example with the View-based Access Control Model in RFC 3415.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: do not answer a note nobody asked for, do not hand out your secret, change the secret every so often, and keep the list of who is allowed locked up.

messages.label: Request, noAuthNoPriv
messages.note: Zero-length user name and engine ID, empty variable list.

messages.label: Authenticated Request
messages.note: Learned engine ID, boots and time set to zero, valid user name.

messages.label: Report
messages.note: Carries current boots and time and usmStatsNotInTimeWindows.

viz.caption: USM SECURITY PARAMETERS, ASN.1 (ABRIDGED FROM THE RFC)

data.title: UsmSecurityParameters
data.code:
UsmSecurityParameters ::=
    SEQUENCE {
        msgAuthoritativeEngineID     OCTET STRING,
        msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots  INTEGER (0..2147483647),
        msgAuthoritativeEngineTime   INTEGER (0..2147483647),
        msgUserName                  OCTET STRING (SIZE(0..32)),
        msgAuthenticationParameters  OCTET STRING,
        msgPrivacyParameters         OCTET STRING
    }
